l: Jehoram, The Second Book of Kings
s: The records merge two kings named Jehoram (also Joram): the son of Ahab, who ruled Israel from Samaria for twelve years, and the son of Jehoshaphat, who ruled Judah from Jerusalem for eight years. Israel's Jehoram did evil, though less than his parents, removed Baal's pillar, and kept Jeroboam's sins. He campaigned against Moab with Jehoshaphat and Edom's king, was rebuked by Elisha, heeded Elisha's warnings, spared captured Syrians with a feast, and wore sackcloth during the siege. Judah's Jehoram married Ahab's daughter, followed the ways of Israel's kings and Ahab's house, did evil, struck Edomites at Zair but could not end their revolt, was buried in David's city, and was succeeded by Ahaziah.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoshaphat is a king of Judah and father of Jehoash. He allies with Jehoram against Moab, pledging his people and horses, asks for a prophet of the LORD, and Elisha helps only out of respect for him.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Judah is the southern kingdom, a political and religious community ruled by a succession of kings, whose story is one of decline, judgment, and exile. Early on, under Jehoram and Ahaziah, it does evil, yet the LORD spares it for David's sake while Edom and Libnah revolt. Under Amaziah it is defeated by Israel at Beth Shemesh, and the people then make young Azariah king. After Israel is removed, Judah remains the only tribe left, but it too is warned by every prophet and seer, fails to keep the commandments, and walks in Israel's statutes. Manasseh leads it into idolatry worse than the nations the LORD destroyed, and the LORD announces coming evil. Josiah's inquiry and covenant reading bring cleansing of high places from Geba to Beersheba, but the LORD still declares he will remove Judah from his sight because of Manasseh's provocation. Tribute to Pharaoh Necoh and evil kings Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim follow. Raiding bands and Babylon subject it, Jehoiachin and leading people are taken captive, and Zedekiah rebels. Finally Judah is carried away, officials are executed at Riblah, and after Gedaliah's murder the remaining people flee to Egypt.

l: Ahaziah's sickness, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahaziah's sickness results from his fall through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria and prompts him to inquire of Baal Zebub about recovery. The LORD declares through Elijah that he will not come down from his bed but will surely die, and the king dies of it as foretold.

l: Elisha, The Second Book of Kings
s: Elisha, son of Shaphat, is a prophet of the LORD and man of God who begins as the servant of Elijah, pouring water on his hands and calling him master. He refuses three times to leave Elijah, asks for a double portion of his spirit, sees him taken up, and cries 'My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!' He takes up Elijah's mantle, parts the Jordan, and is recognized by the sons of the prophets as having Elijah's spirit. He then heals Jericho's waters and curses mocking youths, returning via Mount Carmel to Samaria. His ministry is marked by wonders and by the LORD's word, which Jehoshaphat acknowledges. He prophesies water and victory over Moab, multiplies a widow's oil, promises the Shunammite woman a son and revives the boy by prayer, neutralizes poisoned stew, and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves. He directs Naaman to wash in the Jordan seven times and refuses his gift, swearing by the LORD. He perceives the deceit of his servant Gehazi and passes Naaman's leprosy to him and his offspring. He makes a lost ax head float, reveals the Syrian king's private plans to the king of Israel, prays that his servant's eyes be opened and the Syrian army blinded, then leads them to Samaria and has them fed rather than struck. He foresees a threatening messenger and tells the elders to hold the door shut. He announces cheap flour and barley in Samaria's gate, and the doubting captain sees it but does not eat of it. He warns the Shunammite woman to leave for seven years of famine and tells Hazael that Benhadad will die and that Hazael will be king over Syria, weeping over the violence to come. He sends a young prophet with a vial of oil to anoint Jehu king over Israel. At the end he falls sick with the illness of which he dies. King Joash weeps over him, echoing the same cry he once made for Elijah. Elisha has the king shoot an arrow of victory over Syria, then grows angry when the king strikes the ground only three times. He dies and is buried in a tomb, and a man who touches his bones revives.

l: Bethel, The Second Book of Kings
s: has_altar_built_by Jeroboam [broken down by Josiah] Josiah carries the ashes of the burned idolatrous vessels to Bethel. There he breaks down and burns the altar and high place made by Jeroboam son of Nebat, and burns bones from the tombs on the altar to defile it, fulfilling the word of the man of God. He leaves the tomb of that man of God undisturbed.

l: Jericho, The Second Book of Kings
s: has_inhabitants_description pleasant situation [before the healing, water bad and land barren] Jericho is a stopping point where the sons of the prophets warn Elisha that Elijah will be taken, and where Elisha later stays while the fifty men search in vain. Its men tell Elisha that the city's location is pleasant but its water is bad and the land barren, and Elisha heals the water.

l: Jordan, The Second Book of Kings
s: The Jordan is a river in Israel, where wood-cutting trees grow and beams were cut. It first parts for Elijah's mantle, then for Elisha, who invokes the LORD. Later Elisha sends Naaman to wash there seven times; after scorning Israel's waters, he obeys and is healed.

l: sons of the prophets, The Second Book of Kings
s: Groups of prophets' followers at Bethel and Jericho warn Elisha his master will be taken that day. Fifty watch the Jordan, acknowledge Elijah's spirit on Elisha and bow, then persuade him to let fifty men search three days, finding nothing.

l: mantle (Elijah's mantle), The Second Book of Kings
s: Elijah rolls up his mantle and strikes the Jordan to divide it. It falls from him when he is taken up, and Elisha picks it up and uses it to strike the Jordan, which divides for him.

l: chariot of fire and horses of fire, The Second Book of Kings
s: A chariot of fire and horses of fire appear and separate Elijah from Elisha as they walk and talk. Elijah then goes up by a whirlwind into heaven.

l: spring of the waters (Jericho's spring), The Second Book of Kings
s: has_state healed [healed by Elisha's word] Elisha goes out to the spring of Jericho's waters and throws salt from a new jar into it. He declares in the LORD's name that the waters are healed and will no longer bring death or barrenness.

l: youths of Bethel, The Second Book of Kings
s: Youths come out of the city as Elisha goes up to Bethel and mock him, repeatedly saying 'Go up, you baldy!' Elisha curses them in the LORD's name, and forty-two of them are mauled by bears.

l: two female bears, The Second Book of Kings
s: mauled youths of Bethel [forty-two of them, after Elisha cursed them] Two female bears come out of the woods after Elisha curses the mocking youths in the LORD's name. They maul forty-two of the youths.

l: healing of Jericho's waters, The Second Book of Kings
s: performed_by Elisha [by throwing salt into the spring] At the request of the city's men, Elisha has a new jar of salt brought and throws the salt into the spring, saying the LORD has healed the waters. The text says the waters remained healed to this day, according to Elisha's word.

l: double portion of Elijah's spirit, The Second Book of Kings
s: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit before Elijah is taken, and Elijah calls it a hard thing, granted only if Elisha sees him taken. Elisha sees him go, and afterward the Jordan parts for him and the sons of the prophets say Elijah's spirit rests on him.

l: Mesha, The Second Book of Kings
s: Mesha, king of Moab and a sheep breeder, paid Israel tribute of one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams, rebelled after Ahab died, and, losing the battle and failing to break through to Edom, sacrificed his eldest son on the wall.

l: Jezebel, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jezebel, a king's daughter and mother of Joram, is blamed for shedding the LORD's servants' blood. Prophecy foretells her death; she defiantly taunts Jehu, is thrown down by eunuchs and trampled, leaving only skull, feet, and palms.

l: Baal, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehu pretends that Ahab served Baal a little but he will serve him much, and calls a great sacrifice to Baal as a deception. Baal's pillar is broken and Jehu is said to destroy Baal out of Israel.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Kings
s: Edom is a territory and kingdom bordering Judah. Its king joins Israel and Judah's wilderness expedition, where water comes by way of Edom. Later, in Jehoram's days, Edom revolts from Judah and sets up its own king; Jehoram strikes at Zair, yet Edom remains free.

l: Moabite rebellion against Israel (Moab's revolt), The Second Book of Kings
s: After Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against Israel, ending the supply of lambs and wool he had provided. This revolt prompted Jehoram to muster Israel and call on Jehoshaphat.

l: campaign against Moab (three kings' expedition), The Second Book of Kings
s: Israel, Judah, and Edom marched seven days by a circuitous route and ran out of water, then consulted Elisha. After the miraculous water, they routed Moab, ravaged the land, and besieged Kir Hareseth, but withdrew after Mesha's sacrifice brought great wrath against Israel.

l: water (miraculous water in the valley), The Second Book of Kings
s: Elisha prophesied that the trench-filled valley would fill with water without wind or rain. The next morning, about the time of the sacrifice, water came by way of Edom and filled the country. The sun made it look red as blood to the Moabites, who were deceived into attacking.

l: Mesha's oldest son, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_son_of Mesha [heir who would have reigned] Mesha's oldest son, who would have reigned in his father's place, was taken by Mesha and offered as a burnt offering on the wall.

l: burnt offering (child sacrifice on the wall), The Second Book of Kings
s: Mesha offered his oldest son as a burnt offering on the wall of Kir Hareseth after failing to break through. Great wrath came against Israel, and they departed and returned to their land.

l: Gehazi, The Second Book of Kings
s: Gehazi is the servant of Elisha. In Chapter 4 he acts as Elisha's messenger to the Shunammite woman: relaying Elisha's offer, noting she has no son, trying to push her away at Carmel, carrying Elisha's staff to the dead child, and reporting no awakening. In Chapter 5 he deceitfully takes two talents of silver and clothing from Naaman after Elisha refused a gift, lies to Elisha, and is cursed with leprosy, white as snow, passing to his offspring forever. In Chapter 8 he tells the king of Elisha's deeds and identifies the woman and her son as those Elisha restored to life.

l: Shunammite woman, The Second Book of Kings
s: A prominent woman of Shunem, married to an old husband, who regards Elisha as a holy man of God. She hosts him and suggests building him a roof room. Though doubtful, she bears the son he promises. When the boy dies she lays him on Elisha's bed, rides to Carmel, clings to Elisha's feet, and receives her revived son. Obeying Elisha, she lives seven years in the Philistines' land, then petitions the king, who restores her house, land, and produce.

l: widow of the prophet, The Second Book of Kings
s: A widowed wife of a prophet's son, whose husband feared the LORD, faces a creditor threatening to enslave her two sons. She cries to Elisha, fills borrowed containers with oil from her only pot as instructed, then sells it, pays the debt, and lives on the remainder.

l: pot of oil (the widow's pot of oil), The Second Book of Kings
s: The pot of oil is the only thing the widow has in her house. It supplies oil to fill all the borrowed containers until no more containers are available, and then the oil stops flowing.

l: sons of the prophets, The Second Book of Kings
s: sit_before Elisha [at Gilgal] The sons of the prophets are the group to which the widow's late husband belonged, and they sit before Elisha at Gilgal during a famine. They eat stew made with unrecognized wild gourds, cry out that there is death in the pot, and then eat safely after Elisha adds meal.

l: son (the Shunammite's son), The Second Book of Kings
s: The Shunammite's son is born at the season Elisha foretold. When grown, he cries "My head!" in the field with the reapers, is carried to his mother, sits on her knees until noon and dies. After Elisha's prayer and stretching himself on him, the boy's flesh grows warm, he sneezes seven times, and opens his eyes.

l: stew pot (Elisha's large pot), The Second Book of Kings
s: Elisha has his servant set the large pot on to boil stew for the sons of the prophets. Wild gourds cut into it make the men cry out that there is death in the pot, but after Elisha throws in meal there is nothing harmful in it.

l: first fruits bread, The Second Book of Kings
s: First fruits bread is twenty barley loaves and fresh grain ears a man from Baal Shalishah brings Elisha; Elisha orders it given to the people, and it feeds a hundred men with leftovers, as the LORD said.

l: resurrection of the Shunammite's son, The Second Book of Kings
s: After Gehazi's staff fails, Elisha shuts the door, prays, and stretches himself on the dead child twice; the boy warms, sneezes seven times, opens his eyes, and is given back to the Shunammite.

l: Naaman, The Second Book of Kings
s: Naaman is a valiant captain of the Syrian king's army, credited with a victory the LORD gave Syria, yet afflicted with leprosy. He travels to Israel seeking healing, is angered by Elisha's simple instruction to wash in the Jordan, but heeds his servants, dips seven times, and is cleansed. He then confesses the God of Israel, refuses to give a gift, takes earth, vows worship of the LORD alone, and asks pardon for bowing in Rimmon's house.

l: king of Syria, The Second Book of Kings
s: rules Syria The king of Syria honors Naaman, whose leadership brought Syria victory. On hearing about the prophet in Samaria, he sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel and ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing, asking that Naaman be healed.

l: king of Israel, The Second Book of Kings
s: rules Israel The king of Israel reads the Syrian king's letter and tears his clothes, asking whether he is God to kill and make alive, and suspecting that Syria seeks a quarrel with him. Elisha then sends word asking why he tore his clothes and telling him to let Naaman come to him.

l: little girl (Naaman's wife's servant), The Second Book of Kings
s: A little girl captured from Israel by Syrian bands serves Naaman's wife; she says the prophet in Samaria would heal her lord's leprosy, and her words reach the king, setting events in motion.

l: Syria, The Second Book of Kings
s: Syria oppressed Israel under Hazael, and its king destroyed Jehoahaz's forces, making them like dust in threshing. Elisha foretold that Israel would strike the Syrians at Aphek, and because the king struck the ground only three times, Syria would be defeated just three times. Jehoash then struck Benhadad three times.

l: Syrians, The Second Book of Kings
s: The Syrians are an enemy force opposing Israel. Elisha's warnings let Israel's king avoid their raids; after being fed in Samaria, the bands stop raiding, though Benhadad later besieges Samaria. Finally, hearing a Lord-caused sound of chariots, they panic, flee at twilight, and abandon their camp and goods.

l: Damascus, The Second Book of Kings
s: captured_by Tiglath Pileser [people carried captive to Kir] Damascus was taken by the king of Assyria, who carried its people captive to Kir and killed Rezin. Ahaz went there to meet Tiglath Pileser and saw the altar that was there.

l: leprosy, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_cleansed_by Jordan [washing seven times] Leprosy afflicts Naaman despite his greatness, and he is healed of it after dipping seven times in the Jordan. It is then transferred to Gehazi as punishment for his greed and lying, with Elisha declaring that it will cling to him and his offspring forever.

l: gift to Elisha (Naaman's offering), The Second Book of Kings
s: offered_by Naaman [refused by Elisha] After being healed, Naaman urges Elisha to accept a gift from him. Elisha swears by the LORD that he will receive none and refuses even when pressed.

l: talents of silver and clothing (Gehazi's request), The Second Book of Kings
s: Gehazi falsely asks Naaman for a talent of silver and two changes of clothing in Elisha's name for two supposed visitors. Naaman presses two talents of silver in two bags and two changes of clothing on him, and servants carry them until Gehazi takes them and stores them in his house. Elisha's rebuke over this wealth leads to Gehazi's affliction with leprosy.

l: king of Syria, The Second Book of Kings
s: Benhadad, king of Syria, is at war with Israel. His plans are foiled because Elisha exposes them; he sends an army to seize Elisha at Dothan, then gathers his whole army and besieges Samaria.

l: Syrian army (sent against Elisha), The Second Book of Kings
s: A great army of horses and chariots sent by the king of Syria surrounds Dothan by night to seize Elisha, is struck blind, led to Samaria, restored, fed, and sent home unharmed.

l: servant of Elisha, The Second Book of Kings
s: Elisha's servant rises early, sees the army around Dothan, and cries out in fear to Elisha. Elisha prays, and the LORD opens the young man's eyes so he sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.

l: horses and chariots of fire, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_located_at mountain around Elisha Horses and chariots of fire fill the mountain around Elisha when the LORD opens his servant's eyes. They show that those with Elisha are more than those with the Syrians.

l: siege of Samaria, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_conducted_by king of Syria [Benhadad] After the earlier episode, Benhadad king of Syria gathers all his army and besieges Samaria. The siege causes extreme famine and leads to the woman's appeal to the king on the wall.

l: famine in Samaria, The Second Book of Kings
s: A great famine afflicts the city of Samaria, driving prices for scraps to extreme heights, then pushing two women to boil and eat a son, which horrifies the king, who tears his clothes.

l: woman who appealed to the king, The Second Book of Kings
s: has_child sons of the two women [her son was boiled and eaten] She cries out to the king of Israel on the wall for help. She tells him that she and another woman agreed to eat her son one day and the other's son the next, but after they ate hers the other woman hid her son.

l: sons of the two women, The Second Book of Kings
s: The first woman's son is boiled and eaten during the famine, as agreed with the other woman. The other woman's son is hidden by his mother rather than given up to be eaten.

l: captain (on whose hand the king leaned), The Second Book of Kings
s: A captain serving the king of Israel, on whose hand the king leaned, scoffs at Elisha's prophecy that windows in heaven could bring plenty. The king appoints him over Samaria's gate, where the people trample him to death, as foretold.

l: king of Israel, The Second Book of Kings
s: The king rises in the night after hearing the lepers' report and suspects the Syrians are hiding in the field to ambush the starving city. He follows a servant's advice to send two chariots with horses to look, and they return confirming the Syrians' flight. He had appointed the captain to be in charge of the gate.

l: four leprous men, The Second Book of Kings
s: Four leprous men at Samaria's gate, facing death either way, surrender to the Syrians and find the camp empty. They feast and hide silver, gold, and clothing, then judge this wrong and report to gatekeepers, informing the king's household.

l: city (Samaria), The Second Book of Kings
s: The city is suffering famine, which leads the lepers to reject entering it. The king fears the Syrians are waiting to take its people alive and get in, but the report proves true that they have fled, and the people go out to plunder.

l: camp of the Syrians, The Second Book of Kings
s: has_state abandoned [tents and animals left behind] The camp is found abandoned at twilight, with horses and donkeys tied and the tents as they were. The lepers take goods from two tents, and the people of the city later plunder it.

l: people (of Samaria), The Second Book of Kings
s: plunders camp of the Syrians The people go out and plunder the camp of the Syrians, so a seah of fine flour sells for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel, according to the Lord's word. In the gate they trample the captain, who dies.

l: king (king who spoke with Gehazi), The Second Book of Kings
s: The king asks Gehazi to tell him all the great things Elisha has done. When the woman begs for her house and land, he questions her and appoints an officer to restore all that was hers and the fruits of the field since she left.

l: Hazael, The Second Book of Kings
s: Hazael begins as servant of Benhadad, sent with gifts to ask Elisha about the king's recovery. Elisha reveals Hazael will become king of Syria and do great evil to Israel. He tells Benhadad he will recover, then smothers him with a wet cloth and reigns. As king he fights Joram and Ahaziah at Ramoth Gilead, attacks Israel's borders, captures Gath, and turns toward Jerusalem until Jehoash pays tribute in holy things and gold. He oppresses Israel through Jehoahaz's days, then dies, succeeded by his son Benhadad.

l: Benhadad, The Second Book of Kings
s: Benhadad, king of Syria, falls sick and sends Hazael to ask the LORD through Elisha; told he will die, he is smothered by Hazael next day.

l: Ahab's house, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahab's house is a royal family doomed by the LORD's prophecy, compared to Jeroboam's house; Jehu is told to strike it avenging the prophets' blood, and Joram and Jezebel die.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jerusalem is the royal city of the kings of Judah, said to be chosen by the LORD as the place for his name, and the records follow it through repeated threats until its fall. Early on it is entered by Jehoash, who breaks down part of its wall and takes treasures. Ahaz reigns there and withstands the siege of Rezin and Pekah. Under Hezekiah, tribute is paid from its temple and palace treasures, and an Assyrian army led by Rabshakeh demands surrender; the LORD promises to defend the city for his own sake and David's, so the king of Assyria will not enter it. Then the tone turns. Manasseh fills it with innocent blood, and the LORD declares he will wipe it like a dish. Josiah reads the covenant there, removes idolatrous objects and keeps a great Passover, yet the LORD says he will still cast off the city. Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah reign. Nebuchadnezzar's servants besiege it and take the king, treasures and craftsmen to Babylon. In Zedekiah's eleventh year famine and a breach come, the walls are broken, houses burned, and the people carried away, leaving only the poorest.

l: Edomite revolt, The Second Book of Kings
s: In Jehoram's reign Edom breaks away from Judah and makes a king over itself. Jehoram crosses to Zair and strikes the Edomites who surround him, but the revolt endures to this day, and Libnah revolts at the same time.

l: Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahaziah, son of Jehoram and Athaliah and son-in-law of Ahab's house, became king of Judah at twenty-two and reigned one year in Jerusalem, doing evil in Ahab's house's way. He joined Joram against Hazael at Ramoth Gilead, then visited wounded Joram in Jezreel. When Jehu came, he fled, was struck in his chariot, died at Megiddo, and was buried in David's city, Jerusalem.

l: Athaliah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Athaliah, mother of Ahaziah, destroyed the royal offspring after her son's death and reigned six years while Joash was hidden; hearing the guard and people, she cried "Treason!" and was seized and slain.

l: Jezreel, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jezreel is where Joram has returned to heal from his wounds and where Ahaziah comes to visit him. Joram and Jezebel are killed there, and Naboth's plot of ground there becomes the place of Joram's body and the fulfillment of the word about Jezebel's remains. Jezreel is where the heads of Ahab's sons are brought and heaped at the gate, and where Jehu addresses the people. There Jehu also strikes the remainder of Ahab's house, great men, friends, and priests.

l: young prophet (son of the prophets sent by Elisha), The Second Book of Kings
s: The young prophet goes to Ramoth Gilead, singles out Jehu among the captains, and pours oil on his head in an inner room. He announces the LORD's anointing of Jehu and the doom of Ahab's house and Jezebel, then opens the door and flees. Jehu's companions later call him a madman.

l: Jehu, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, is anointed king over Israel through a young prophet's message from the LORD. He drives furiously to Jezreel, kills Joram with an arrow, has Ahaziah struck, and has Jezebel thrown down and trampled. He then destroys Ahab's house, Ahaziah's brothers, and Baal's worshipers, removing Baal worship from Israel. Yet he follows Jeroboam's sins and does not wholeheartedly walk in the LORD's law. He reigns twenty-eight years from Samaria, is buried there, and is succeeded by his son Jehoahaz.

l: Naboth the Jezreelite, The Second Book of Kings
s: owns plot of land in Jezreel Naboth's land at Jezreel is where Jehu meets Joram and kills him. Jehu has Joram's body thrown onto that plot, citing the LORD's word that he would repay Ahab there for the blood of Naboth and his sons.

l: Jehu's anointing as king, The Second Book of Kings
s: occurs_at Ramoth Gilead Following Elisha's instructions, the young prophet privately pours oil on Jehu's head at Ramoth Gilead and declares him king over Israel. After Jehu reluctantly repeats the message, the other captains hurry to place their cloaks under him, blow the trumpet, and proclaim him king.

l: Jehu's killing of Joram, The Second Book of Kings
s: occurs_at Jezreel [on Naboth's land] After the watchman reports the furious driving, Jehu meets Joram on Naboth's land and answers his question about peace by pointing to Jezebel's prostitution and witchcraft. He draws his bow and shoots Joram through the heart, then has Bidkar throw the body onto Naboth's plot to fulfill the LORD's word.

l: death of Jezebel, The Second Book of Kings
s: occurs_at Jezreel [fulfilling the word of Elijah] Jezebel looks out the window and taunts Jehu, who calls for support and has two or three eunuchs throw her down. Her blood spatters the wall and horses, and Jehu tramples her. When burial is attempted, only her skull, feet, and palms remain, which Jehu says fulfills Elijah's word.

l: Ahab's sons, The Second Book of Kings
s: located_in Samaria [raised by the great men of the city] Ahab's seventy sons are raised by the great men of Samaria. After Jehu's letters, they are killed and their heads are sent in baskets to Jezreel, where they are laid in two heaps at the gate entrance until morning.

l: rulers and elders of Jezreel and Samaria, The Second Book of Kings
s: The rulers, elders, and guardians of Ahab's sons, fearing Jehu because two kings could not stand before him, declare themselves his servants and refuse to make any man king. They obey his second letter by killing the seventy sons and sending their heads to him.

l: brothers of Ahaziah, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_related_to Ahaziah [brothers; Ahaziah is king of Judah] Forty-two brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah, traveling to greet the children of the king and queen, meet Jehu at the shearing house. He orders them taken alive and they are killed at the pit, with none left.

l: Jehonadab the son of Rechab, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_ally_of Jehu [shared heart, rode in his chariot] Jehonadab meets Jehu, affirms that his heart is right with Jehu's, and is taken up into Jehu's chariot to see his zeal for the LORD. He accompanies Jehu into the house of Baal.

l: worshipers of Baal, The Second Book of Kings
s: All of Baal's prophets, worshipers, and priests are summoned and fill the house of Baal, wearing robes brought out for them. After they offer sacrifices, Jehu's guard and captains kill them all with the sword.

l: house of Baal, The Second Book of Kings
s: became latrine [after being broken down, to this day] The house of Baal is filled from end to end with worshipers, who are killed inside it. Its pillars are burned, and the house is broken down and made a latrine, as it remains to this day.

l: Jehoahaz, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoahaz, son of Josiah and Hamutal, was made king by the people of the land at twenty-three, reigned three months in Jerusalem, did evil in the LORD's sight, was bound by Pharaoh Necoh, and died in Egypt.

l: Ahab's house massacre, The Second Book of Kings
s: fulfills the LORD [the LORD's word spoken by Elijah] Jehu orchestrates the killing of Ahab's seventy sons by their guardians, then strikes all remaining in Ahab's house at Jezreel and Samaria, leaving none. He tells the people they are righteous and that this fulfills the LORD's word by Elijah.

l: Jehosheba, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, rescued Joash from the slain king's sons, hiding him and his nurse, saving him from Athaliah.

l: Jehoash, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoash (also Joash), son of Ahaziah and Zibiah of Beersheba, was hidden in the LORD's house for six years after a slaughter, then crowned king at age seven in the seventh year of Jehu. He reigned forty years in Jerusalem, doing right while the priest Jehoiada instructed him. He ordered temple repairs and confronted the priests when they lagged, but paid Hazael with holy things and gold. His servants struck him down at Millo; he was buried in David's city, succeeded by Amaziah.

l: Jehoiada, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoiada is a priest who leads decisive action for the LORD's house. He gathers captains, covenants with them, crowns Joash, has Athaliah killed, and appoints officers over the house. He then instructs Jehoash, who does right while instructed. When priests fail to repair the house, Jehoiada bores a hole in a chest's lid and sets it beside the altar.

l: captains over hundreds, The Second Book of Kings
s: The captains over hundreds of the Carites and the guard were fetched by Jehoiada, entered a covenant, and did all he commanded, bringing their men to him. They received David's spears and shields, and were ordered to bring Athaliah out between the ranks and kill anyone who followed her.

l: guard, The Second Book of Kings
s: The guard stood with weapons in hand around the king from the right side of the house to the left, along by the altar. They were commanded to slay anyone entering the ranks, and later helped bring the king down to the king's house by the gate of the guard.

l: people of the land, The Second Book of Kings
s: destroys house of Baal [broke it down] The people of the land rejoiced and blew trumpets at Joash's coronation. They then went to the house of Baal, broke down its altars and images, and killed Mattan the priest of Baal, and they accompanied the king to his house; the city was quiet.

l: LORD's house, The Second Book of Kings
s: The LORD's house in Jerusalem is the place where the LORD put his name, promised to David and Solomon. It held King David's spears and shields. Early on it sheltered Joash for six years, hosted the covenant and his crowning, and was guarded by appointed officers. Later it was repaired with collected money, though its treasures were once sent to Hazael. Manasseh defiled it with altars for the army of the sky and an Asherah image in its courts. During another repair Hilkiah found the book of the law there. It ends in ruin: Nebuzaradan burned it, and the Chaldeans broke up its bronze pillars, sea and bases and carried them and its vessels to Babylon.

l: king's house, The Second Book of Kings
s: The king's house was to be guarded by one third of the incoming watch. Athaliah was slain at the horses' entry to it, and Joash was brought there by the gate of the guard to sit on the throne of the kings.

l: Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoiada brought out the king's son, put the crown on him, gave him the covenant, and anointed him while the guard surrounded him. The people clapped and said "Long live the king!", and the king stood by the pillar with captains and trumpets as was the tradition.

l: killing of Athaliah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Athaliah, after crying "Treason!", is seized on Jehoiada's order, led between the ranks away from the LORD's house, and slain with a sword at the king's house.

l: priests, The Second Book of Kings
s: The priests are a group instructed by Jehoash to collect donor money and repair the house, but by his twenty-third year they had not. They then agreed to take no more money and not repair it. Threshold-keeping priests put offerings into the chest; trespass and sin offering money stayed theirs.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Kings
s: status not done by the twenty-third year of Jehoash [priests had not repaired the damage] Jehoash ordered the priests to repair the damage wherever it was found, but it had not been done by his twenty-third year. Once the chest funds were counted and paid out, carpenters, builders, masons, and stone cutters worked on it, and timber and cut stone were bought. All the money went to the workers and the repair.

l: money (temple donations), The Second Book of Kings
s: Temple money brought into the LORD's house, including current money, evaluation money, and voluntary gifts, was meant for repairs. Jehoash first had priests take it, then had them stop and deliver it. It was weighed, bagged, counted, and paid to carpenters, builders, masons, and stone cutters, not silver vessels; trespass and sin offering money stayed with priests.

l: chest (Jehoiada's chest), The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoiada's chest is a lidded container with a hole he bored, placed beside the altar on the right as one enters the LORD's house. Threshold-keeping priests deposited the temple money into it; once full, the king's scribe and high priest bagged and counted it.

l: holy things and treasures, The Second Book of Kings
s: dedicated_by Jehoshaphat [with Jehoram and Ahaziah, Jehoash's fathers] Jehoash took the holy things dedicated by Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, his fathers, along with his own holy things and all the gold in the treasures of the LORD's house and the king's house. He sent all of it to Hazael king of Syria, after which Hazael left Jerusalem.

l: Jehoash's servants, The Second Book of Kings
s: conspired_against Jehoash [struck him at the house of Millo] Jehoash's servants arose, made a conspiracy, and struck him at the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla. Two of them are named as Jozacar and Jehozabad.

l: Jozacar, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jozacar, son of Shimeath, was a servant of Jehoash who, with others, struck Jehoash so that he died.

l: Jehozabad, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_son_of Shomer Jehozabad the son of Shomer was one of Jehoash's servants who struck him so that he died.

l: Amaziah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Amaziah was a king of Judah, son of Joash and Jehoaddin, who began reigning at twenty-five and ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He did right in the LORD's eyes, though not like David, and killed his father's murderers while sparing their children. He struck ten thousand Edomites and captured Sela, but provoked Jehoash of Israel and was defeated at Beth Shemesh. Conspirators killed him at Lachish; he was buried in Jerusalem and Azariah succeeded him.

l: conspiracy against Jehoash, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoash's servants made a conspiracy and struck him at the house of Millo, on the way that goes down to Silla. Jozacar and Jehozabad killed him, he was buried with his fathers in David's city, and Amaziah his son reigned in his place.

l: Jehoahaz the son of Jehu, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, was an evil king of Israel who reigned seventeen years in Samaria, following Jeroboam's sins. The LORD delivered Israel to Hazael and Benhadad; he begged the LORD, who listened, though his army stayed small. He was buried in Samaria and succeeded by his son Jehoash.

l: Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoash (also called Joash), son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu, was king of Israel who reigned sixteen years in Samaria. He did evil in the LORD's sight, walking in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. He wept over the sick Elisha, but struck the ground only three times at Elisha's command, provoking Elisha's anger. He struck Benhadad three times and recovered Israel's cities. Challenged by Amaziah of Judah, he answered with a parable of a thistle and a cedar, then defeated Judah at Beth Shemesh, captured Amaziah, broke down part of Jerusalem's wall, and carried treasures and hostages to Samaria. He died, was buried in Samaria, and was succeeded by his son Jeroboam.

l: Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jeroboam, son of Joash, was a king of Israel who reigned forty-one years in Samaria, beginning in Amaziah's fifteenth year. He did evil in the LORD's sight, following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Yet, by the LORD's will and the prophet Jonah's word, he saved Israel, restored its border from Hamath to the Arabah sea, and recovered Damascus. His son Zechariah succeeded him.

l: Benhadad the son of Hazael, The Second Book of Kings
s: succeeded Hazael king of Syria [as king of Syria] Benhadad was given power over Israel along with his father Hazael, and he reigned after Hazael died. Jehoash took back from him the cities that had been taken from Jehoahaz, striking him three times.

l: man (revived by Elisha's bones), The Second Book of Kings
s: revived_by Elisha [touched Elisha's bones in his tomb] As this man was being buried, the burial party saw a band of raiders and threw him into Elisha's tomb. As soon as he touched Elisha's bones, he revived and stood up on his feet.

l: Azariah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Azariah, son of Amaziah and Jecoliah of Jerusalem, was made king of Judah at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. He built Elath and restored it to Judah and did right in the LORD's eyes. Struck with leprosy until death, he lived apart while his son Jotham managed the household and succeeded him; he was buried in the City of David.

l: Zechariah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, was king of Israel who reigned in Samaria only six months, did evil like Jeroboam son of Nebat, and was publicly struck down and killed by Shallum's conspiracy.

l: Beth Shemesh, The Second Book of Kings
s: belongs_to Judah Beth Shemesh, which belongs to Judah, was the place where Jehoash and Amaziah met face to face. There Judah was defeated and Jehoash took Amaziah captive.

l: battle at Beth Shemesh (Amaziah and Jehoash), The Second Book of Kings
s: has_outcome Judah defeated by Israel After Amaziah refused Jehoash's warning, the two kings faced each other at Beth Shemesh. Judah was defeated by Israel and each man fled to his tent, and Amaziah was captured, leading to Jerusalem's wall being broken and its treasures taken.

l: Jotham, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jotham, son of Azariah and Jerusha, was a king of Judah. He governed the household and judged the people while his father was leprous, then reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem from age twenty-five. He did right but left the high places, built the LORD's upper gate, was buried in the City of David, and was succeeded by Ahaz.

l: Shallum, The Second Book of Kings
s: Shallum, son of Jabesh, conspired against Zechariah, killed him, and reigned in Samaria as king of Israel for one month before Menahem killed him and succeeded him.

l: Menahem, The Second Book of Kings
s: Menahem, son of Gadi, was a king of Israel who killed Shallum, then reigned ten years in Samaria doing evil. He brutally attacked Tiphsah, paid Pul of Assyria a thousand talents of silver raised by taxing wealthy men, and was succeeded by his son Pekahiah.

l: Assyria, The Second Book of Kings
s: Assyria's king besieges and captures Samaria, deports Israel to Halah, the Habor, and the cities of the Medes, and replaces them with peoples from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim. When the settlers suffer lions, he orders one of the exiled priests sent back to teach them the law of the god of the land. Assyria's king and servants are said to have blasphemed the LORD, and its kings are described as having laid waste nations and burned their gods. Its king hears of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia coming out to fight and sends a threatening letter to Hezekiah. Its camp is struck by the LORD's angel with 185,000 dead, and its king returns home and is later assassinated, with Esar Haddon his son reigning in his place.

l: Pekahiah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Pekahiah, son of Menahem, was a king of Israel who reigned two years in Samaria, did evil following Jeroboam's sins, and was killed in a conspiracy by his captain Pekah, who replaced him.

l: Pekah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Pekah, son of Remaliah, was a king of Israel who rose as captain of Pekahiah, killed him, and reigned twenty years in Samaria, doing evil like Jeroboam. Assyria's Tiglath Pileser seized northern lands in his reign. He allied with Rezin of Syria to besiege Ahaz in Jerusalem without success, and Hoshea finally conspired against and killed him.

l: Tiglath Pileser, The Second Book of Kings
s: Tiglath Pileser is a king of Assyria. In Pekah's days he conquered Naphtali and neighboring towns, deporting their people to Assyria. Later Ahaz, calling himself his servant and son, sent silver and gold; he attacked Damascus, took it, deported its people to Kir, and killed Rezin. Ahaz's temple changes followed because of him.

l: Hoshea, The Second Book of Kings
s: Hoshea, son of Elah, was a king of Israel who seized the throne by conspiring against and killing Pekah, then reigned nine years in Samaria. He did evil, though less than earlier kings. He served Shalmaneser of Assyria and paid tribute, but sought help from Egypt's king So and withheld tribute, so Assyria's king seized and imprisoned him.

l: Rezin, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_a king of Syria Rezin king of Syria came up against Jerusalem with Pekah and besieged Ahaz without overcoming him. He recovered Elath for Syria and drove the Jews out, so that Syrians lived there to this day. He was killed when the king of Assyria took Damascus.

l: Ahaz, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahaz, son of Jotham, became king of Judah at twenty and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. Unlike David, he did not do right in the LORD's eyes: he followed Israel's kings, worshipped idolatrously at high places, and made his son pass through the fire. He called himself servant of Tiglath Pileser, paying tribute from the LORD's house and royal treasuries. He had Urijah build a new altar, reserved the bronze altar for himself, and was buried in the City of David, succeeded by Hezekiah.

l: Urijah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Urijah is a priest who, following Ahaz's drawing and plans of the Damascus altar, built a matching altar before Ahaz returned, then obeyed him by offering regular sacrifices on it.

l: Hezekiah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Hezekiah, son of Ahaz and Abi, was a king of Judah who began reigning at twenty-five and ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He did right in the LORD's eyes as David had: removing high places, breaking pillars, cutting down the Asherah, and breaking the bronze serpent Nehushtan. He trusted the LORD, unmatched among Judah's kings, kept the commandments given to Moses, rebelled against Assyria, and struck the Philistines as far as Gaza. When Sennacherib seized Judah's fortified cities, he admitted offense and paid tribute, stripping the temple and palace treasuries and the temple's gold doors. After Rabshakeh's threats, he tore his clothes, wore sackcloth, sought Isaiah's prayer, spread Sennacherib's letter before the LORD, and prayed; the LORD promised to defend Jerusalem and the Assyrian threat ended. Sick with a boil and near death, he prayed, claiming he walked in truth with a perfect heart, and was granted fifteen more years, with the shadow going back ten steps as the sign. He then showed Babylon's envoys all his treasures and armor; Isaiah prophesied Babylonian plunder, and Hezekiah called it good, hoping for peace in his days. He built a pool and conduit bringing water into the city. He died, and his son Manasseh reigned.

l: altar at Damascus, The Second Book of Kings
s: located_in Damascus Ahaz saw this altar at Damascus and sent Urijah a drawing and plans to build one like it. Urijah built it before Ahaz returned, and Ahaz offered his burnt, meal, drink and peace offerings on it. It became the great altar for the morning and evening offerings and those of all the people of the land.

l: bronze altar, The Second Book of Kings
s: located_in house of the LORD [originally before the LORD, later moved to north side of Ahaz's altar] The bronze altar, which stood before the LORD, was moved by Ahaz from the front of the house, from between his new altar and the LORD's house, to the north side of his altar. Ahaz said it would be for him to inquire by.

l: idolatrous worship, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ahaz walked in the way of the kings of Israel, made his son pass through the fire according to the abominations of the nations, and sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on hills and under every green tree. The text also records him replacing the arrangement of temple worship with an altar copied from Damascus.

l: Shalmaneser king of Assyria, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_a king of Assyria Shalmaneser came up against Hoshea and made him a tribute-paying servant. When he discovered Hoshea's conspiracy with So king of Egypt and the withheld tribute, the king of Assyria seized and imprisoned Hoshea.

l: Babylon, The Second Book of Kings
s: Babylon is a distant, rising power whose king first sends envoys to Hezekiah, prompting Isaiah's prophecy that Judah's treasures and some of Hezekiah's sons will be taken there. Under Nebuchadnezzar it takes over Egypt's former territory, receives Jehoiachin and Jerusalem's deportees, and installs Zedekiah, who rebels. Ultimately Zedekiah is carried there in fetters, the temple bronze is taken, and Jehoiachin is honored.

l: foreign settlers in Samaria, The Second Book of Kings
s: Foreign settlers from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim were placed by Assyria in Samaria's cities in place of the Israelites. Initially not fearing the LORD, they suffered lion attacks, then a returned priest at Bethel taught them. They nonetheless kept making their own gods and high-place priests, continuing this mixed worship to this day.

l: idolatry and high-place worship, The Second Book of Kings
s: Idolatry and high-place worship, forbidden by the LORD, involves pillars and Asherah poles on every hill and under every tree. Israel practiced it widely, including child sacrifice, which the text gives as the reason for its exile; foreign settlers then repeat it while fearing the LORD.

l: siege and fall of Samaria, The Second Book of Kings
s: Assyria's king Shalmaneser, after discovering Hoshea's conspiracy, invaded the land and besieged Samaria for three years, capturing it in Hoshea's ninth year.

l: exile of Israel to Assyria, The Second Book of Kings
s: In Hoshea's ninth year, Assyria's king carried Israel away, settling them in Halah, on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in Median cities. Caused by sin against the LORD, it fulfills prophetic warnings; Israel remains exiled.

l: Sennacherib, The Second Book of Kings
s: Sennacherib is king of Assyria. In Hezekiah's fourteenth year he captured Judah's fortified cities, took silver and gold from Hezekiah, and sent Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh with a great army from Lachish to Jerusalem. He then sent a letter defying the LORD, who rebuked his arrogance and promised to turn him back. He departed to Nineveh and was killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshiping Nisroch.

l: Rabshakeh, The Second Book of Kings
s: Rabshakeh is the Assyrian envoy serving Sennacherib's king. Sent with Tartan and Rabsaris, he stands by the upper pool and shouts in the Jews' language to the wall's people, mocking Hezekiah's trust in Egypt and the LORD and offering peace and resettlement. His words defying God alarm Hezekiah; he then rejoins the king at Libnah.

l: Eliakim, The Second Book of Kings
s: Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, oversees Hezekiah's household. With Shebnah and Joah he meets Rabshakeh, asks him to speak Syrian rather than the Jews' language before the people on the wall, then reports Rabshakeh's words to Hezekiah in torn clothes.

l: Hilkiah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Hilkiah is a high priest who counts the money brought into the LORD's house, finds the book of the law and gives it to Shaphan, then is sent by the king to inquire of the LORD through Huldah.

l: Rabshakeh's speech, The Second Book of Kings
s: Rabshakeh's speech is a persuasive address urging Judah to surrender to Assyria. He mocks Hezekiah's confidence, calls Egypt a bruised reed, notes Hezekiah removed the LORD's high places, and claims the LORD sent Assyria to destroy the land. He offers horses mockingly, promises a land of grain, wine and honey for peace, and cites fallen gods as proof. The people answer nothing.

l: Isaiah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Isaiah, a prophet and son of Amoz, serves as the LORD's messenger to King Hezekiah. First he reassures Hezekiah's messengers about Assyria, rebukes Sennacherib, and promises the city will be spared. Then he announces Hezekiah's death, returns to declare healing and fifteen added years, applies a fig cake and moves the shadow back. Finally he prophesies that Hezekiah's house will be carried to Babylon.

l: slaughter of the Assyrian camp, The Second Book of Kings
s: The LORD's angel strikes down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp in one night; men rising at dawn find corpses, fulfilling the promise Jerusalem would not fall, and Sennacherib returns to Nineveh.

l: Hezekiah's prayer, The Second Book of Kings
s: Hezekiah's prayer, offered in the LORD's house, addresses the LORD as God of Israel enthroned above the cherubim and maker of heaven and earth. He asks salvation from Sennacherib so all kingdoms know the LORD alone is God; the LORD answers through Isaiah that he heard.

l: Berodach Baladan, The Second Book of Kings
s: Berodach Baladan, son of Baladan and king of Babylon, rules Babylon and sends letters and a gift to Hezekiah after hearing of his sickness.

l: Babylonian envoys (sent by Berodach Baladan), The Second Book of Kings
s: come_from Babylon [a far country] The envoys bring letters and a present from Berodach Baladan to Hezekiah. Hezekiah listens to them and shows them his storehouse, silver, gold, spices, precious oil, armory, and everything in his treasures and dominion.

l: Hezekiah's sickness (boil), The Second Book of Kings
s: is_treated_with cake of figs [laid on the boil] Hezekiah's illness is first declared fatal by Isaiah. After his prayer, the LORD promises healing, and a cake of figs laid on the boil leads to his recovery. He is promised he will go up to the LORD's house on the third day.

l: Hezekiah's treasures, The Second Book of Kings
s: will_be_carried_to Babylon [prophesied by Isaiah; nothing will be left] Hezekiah's treasures include silver, gold, spices, precious oil, his armory, and everything in his storehouses, all of which he shows to the Babylonian envoys. Isaiah prophesies that all of it, along with what his fathers stored, will be carried to Babylon with nothing left.

l: Manasseh, The Second Book of Kings
s: Manasseh was a king of Judah, son of Hezekiah and Hephzibah, who took the throne at twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the LORD's sight: he rebuilt the high places Hezekiah had destroyed, built altars for Baal and the army of the sky, even in the LORD's house, made an Asherah, sacrificed his son in fire, practiced sorcery, and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. He led Judah into sin with his idols, and the LORD would not pardon. He was buried in the garden of Uzza and succeeded by his son Amon.

l: Amon, The Second Book of Kings
s: Amon, son of Manasseh and Meshullemeth, became king of Judah at twenty-two and reigned two years in Jerusalem. Like his father, he did evil, served idols, and abandoned the LORD. His servants conspired and killed him in his own house. He was buried in the garden of Uzza, succeeded by his son Josiah.

l: Josiah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Josiah was a righteous king of Judah who took the throne at age eight, son of Jedidah, and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem, following David's example. Hearing the book of the law, he tore his clothes and inquired of the LORD; through Huldah he learned that, because he was tender-hearted and humbled himself, he would be spared the coming judgment. He gathered the people, read the covenant, made a covenant to keep the LORD's commandments, destroyed idolatrous objects and high places, killed priests of the high places in Samaria, and commanded the Passover. No king before or after turned to the LORD as he did. Father of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim, he was killed by Pharaoh Necoh at Megiddo and buried in his own tomb in Jerusalem.

l: servants of Amon, The Second Book of Kings
s: conspire_against Amon [killed him in his house] The servants of Amon conspired against him and put the king to death in his own house. The people of the land then killed all of those who had conspired.

l: people of the land, The Second Book of Kings
s: The people of the land avenge King Amon by killing his conspirators, then install his son Josiah as king in his place.

l: coming judgment on Jerusalem and Judah, The Second Book of Kings
s: The LORD decrees disaster on Jerusalem and Judah because of Manasseh's abominations and leading Judah into sin. Announced through prophets, it will make hearers' ears tingle: Jerusalem measured by Samaria's line and Ahab's plumb line, wiped like an upturned dish, and the remnant given to enemies as plunder, for provoking him since Egypt.

l: Shaphan, The Second Book of Kings
s: Shaphan, a scribe and son of Azaliah, is sent by Josiah to Hilkiah about temple money, receives and reads the law book, reports to the king, reads it aloud, and is sent to Huldah.

l: book of the covenant, The Second Book of Kings
s: The book of the covenant, also called the book of the law, was found by Hilkiah in the LORD's house. Shaphan read it before the king, and Josiah tore his clothes, recognizing the LORD's wrath because their fathers disobeyed it. Huldah confirmed its evil would come. Josiah then read it to all the people, made a covenant, kept the Passover, and removed idols as it commanded.

l: temple repair, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_funded_by money for the temple repairs Josiah orders money to be given to the workers overseeing the LORD's house for carpenters, builders, masons, and for timber and cut stone. No accounting is required of them because they deal faithfully. The discovery of the book occurs in the course of this work.

l: Huldah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Huldah, a prophetess married to Shallum and living in Jerusalem's second quarter, is consulted by royal officials and delivers the LORD's word: coming evil on the place, peace for Josiah.

l: God's coming judgment, The Second Book of Kings
s: God's coming judgment on Jerusalem and the LORD's house, declared through Huldah: the LORD will bring evil matching the book's words, with unquenchable wrath, because the people forsook him for other gods; Josiah is spared seeing it due to humility.

l: Passover, The Second Book of Kings
s: Passover is a covenant observance Josiah commands all the people to keep, as written in the book of the covenant. Held in Jerusalem in his eighteenth year, it is described as unmatched since the judges or any kings of Israel or Judah.

l: Pharaoh Necoh, The Second Book of Kings
s: Pharaoh Necoh, king of Egypt, marches against Assyria's king, kills Josiah at Megiddo, imprisons Jehoahaz at Riblah and takes him to Egypt, imposes silver-and-gold tribute on Judah, and installs Eliakim as king, renaming him Jehoiakim.

l: Jehoiakim, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoiakim, formerly Eliakim, son of Josiah and Zebidah, is made king of Judah by Pharaoh Necoh, who renames him. At twenty-five he begins an eleven-year reign in Jerusalem, taxing the people to pay Pharaoh's tribute and doing evil in the LORD's sight. He serves Nebuchadnezzar three years, then rebels; the LORD sends raiding bands against Judah. He dies and his son Jehoiachin succeeds him.

l: covenant, The Second Book of Kings
s: Standing by the pillar, Josiah makes a covenant before the LORD to walk after him and keep his commandments, testimonies, and statutes with all his heart and soul, confirming the words written in the book. All the people agree to the covenant.

l: Josiah's religious reforms, The Second Book of Kings
s: Josiah's religious reforms are a sweeping purge of idolatry, aimed at confirming the words of the law in the book Hilkiah found. He removes Baal, Asherah and sky-army vessels, idolatrous priests and shrines, defiles Topheth and the high places, burns the sun chariots, destroys the Bethel altar, and extends the purge to Samaria, yet the LORD's wrath against Judah is not turned.

l: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, The Second Book of Kings
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, holds territory from the brook of Egypt to the Euphrates, taken from Egypt's king. He attacks Judah after Jehoiakim's rebellion, captures Jehoiachin, plunders the temple and royal treasures, and deports the leading people, including ten thousand captives. He installs Zedekiah as king. Later he besieges Jerusalem, his captain Nebuzaradan destroys it, and he leaves Gedaliah as governor over those remaining in Judah.

l: Jehoiachin king of Judah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Jehoiachin was a king of Judah who succeeded Jehoiakim at eighteen and reigned only three months in Jerusalem. His mother was Nehushta, and he did evil like his father. He surrendered to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, princes and officers, and was captured by Nebuchadnezzar and carried to Babylon. In the thirty-seventh year of captivity, Evilmerodach released him, spoke kindly, set his throne above other kings, and gave him a daily allowance for life.

l: Zedekiah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Zedekiah, originally named Mattaniah, was the uncle of Jehoiachin and was installed as king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who changed his name. He began reigning at twenty-one and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem, doing evil like Jehoiakim and rebelling against Babylon. When the city was breached he fled by night, but the Chaldeans overtook him near Jericho. At Riblah his sons were killed before him, he was blinded, fettered, and carried to Babylon.

l: Chaldeans, The Second Book of Kings
s: The Chaldeans surrounded the city, pursued and captured Zedekiah, and under Nebuzaradan broke down Jerusalem's walls and broke up the bronze of the LORD's house to carry it to Babylon. Some Chaldeans were with Gedaliah at Mizpah and were killed with him, and the people later fled to Egypt in fear of them.

l: captives of Jerusalem (carried by Nebuchadnezzar), The Second Book of Kings
s: includes princes, mighty men of valor, craftsmen and smiths [ten thousand captives] Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem, including the princes, ten thousand captives, mighty men of valor, craftsmen and smiths, with only the poorest left. The text also gives seven thousand men of might and one thousand craftsmen and smiths, all strong and fit for war, brought captive to Babylon. Jehoiachin, the king's mother, wives, officers and chief men were among them.

l: Babylonian exile/deportation of Judah, The Second Book of Kings
s: The Babylonian exile of Judah was the captive removal of Judah's people from their land, framed as the LORD's doing. In Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year, after Jehoiachin surrendered, Babylon took temple and palace treasures and deported the king, household, officials, warriors and craftsmen. Nebuzaradan later carried away the remaining people, leaving only the poorest. It closes with Jehoiachin released from prison.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings
s: occurs_in Jerusalem [Nebuchadnezzar came while servants besieged it] Nebuchadnezzar's servants came up and besieged Jerusalem, and Nebuchadnezzar himself arrived while they were besieging it. It ended when Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, princes and officers and was captured.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings
s: lasts_until eleventh year of King Zedekiah The siege began on the tenth day of the tenth month of Nebuchadnezzar's ninth year, with the Babylonians building forts around the city. It lasted until Zedekiah's eleventh year, when famine left no bread for the people and a breach was made in the city.

l: Nebuzaradan, The Second Book of Kings
s: is_a captain of the guard [servant of the king of Babylon] Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard and servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem on the seventh day of the fifth month and burned the LORD's house, the king's house and the great houses. He carried away the remaining people, left some of the poorest, took the temple's bronze, gold and silver, and brought Seraiah, Zephaniah and other officials to the king at Riblah.

l: Gedaliah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, was appointed governor over Judah's remaining people by Nebuchadnezzar. At Mizpah he reassured the captains to stay and serve Babylon, but in the seventh month Ishmael killed him, along with those with him.

l: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, The Second Book of Kings
s: Ishmael, son of Nethaniah and of royal offspring, was a captain who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah, then in the seventh month killed him with ten men, plus Jews and Chaldeans.

l: Evilmerodach king of Babylon, The Second Book of Kings
s: releases Jehoiachin king of Judah [from prison, in the year he began to reign] In the year he began to reign, Evilmerodach released Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison. He spoke kindly to him, set his throne above those of the kings with him in Babylon, and gave him a continual daily allowance for life.

l: burning and destruction of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Kings
s: On the seventh day of the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, Nebuzaradan burned the LORD's house, the king's house, all the houses of Jerusalem and every great house. The Chaldean army broke down the walls around the city.

l: The Book of Job
s: This document is the book of Job, a dialogue-driven narrative about a blameless, wealthy man in the land of Uz and the question of why he suffers. In the opening chapters the LORD allows Satan to test Job. Job loses his livestock, servants and all ten children, then is struck with painful sores. He refuses his wife's urging to renounce God and does not sin with his lips. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, come to comfort him and sit silently with him for seven days. Job then breaks the silence by cursing the day of his birth and longing for death. The middle of the book is three cycles of speeches. The friends argue that God is just, that the wicked are punished and the innocent do not perish, and so Job must have sinned and should repent. Job rejects this. He maintains his integrity, notes that the wicked often prosper, accuses God of wearing him down, longs for an umpire or a hearing with God, and declares confidence that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God. Bildad's final reply is brief, and Job answers with praise of God's power. He then insists on his righteousness, offers a hymn that wisdom is found only in the fear of the Lord, recalls his former honor, laments his present humiliation, and swears a long series of oaths of innocence, demanding that the Almighty answer. A new speaker, Elihu, angry at Job for justifying himself and at the friends for failing to answer him, argues that God is just and greater than man, speaks through dreams and suffering to turn people from the pit, and reveals his power in nature. The LORD then answers Job out of the whirlwind with questions about creation, the heavens, and wild animals, which show the limits of Job's knowledge. Job, after a first reply that he is of small account, hears more about behemoth and Leviathan. He acknowledges that the LORD can do all things, admits he spoke of what he did not understand, and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly as Job did, and has them offer sacrifices while Job prays for them. The LORD restores Job's prosperity at twice what he had before, along with seven sons and three daughters. Job lives one hundred forty more years and dies old and full of days.

l: Job, The Book of Job
s: Job is a blameless, upright, God-fearing man of Uz, called 'my servant' by the LORD. He is the greatest of the children of the east, with seven sons, three daughters, vast livestock, and a very great household. He continually offers burnt offerings for his children. In a series of disasters he loses his livestock, servants, and all his children, yet he worships, blesses the LORD's name, and does not charge God with wrongdoing. Struck with painful sores from head to foot, he sits in ashes, rebukes his wife, and still does not sin with his lips. The records stress that he keeps his integrity throughout. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, come to him. Job then curses the day of his birth, sighs and groans, and wishes God would crush him, though he takes consolation that he has not denied the Holy One's words. In his replies he calls his friends miserable comforters and deceitful brothers, claims understanding equal to theirs, and insists his cause is righteous. He feels watched, worn out, treated as an enemy, and set in stocks by God. He longs for an umpire, a witness in heaven, and a Redeemer, and expects to see God in his flesh. He wants to reason with God and believes he will come out like gold, yet he is terrified before God and cannot find him. He swears he will hold fast to his righteousness until death. He recalls his former standing: he delivered the poor and fatherless, was eyes to the blind, sat as chief, and was honored by listeners. In his final defense he lists his faithfulness and challenges the Almighty to answer. When the three friends stop answering, Elihu grows angry, quoting Job as claiming he is righteous, and accuses him of rebellion, empty talk and justifying himself rather than God. The LORD then addresses Job as one who darkens counsel by words without knowledge and asks long questions about creation, behemoth and Leviathan. Job calls himself of small account, lays his hand on his mouth, confesses he spoke of things he did not understand, and repents in dust and ashes. The LORD calls him his servant, says he spoke rightly, and accepts his prayer for his three friends. Job is restored with twice his former wealth, has seven sons and three daughters again, lives one hundred forty more years, sees four generations, and dies old and full of days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Job
s: The LORD is the sovereign God who figures in Job's story. He first appears receiving God's sons and Satan, pointing out Job as blameless and upright. He permits Satan to take all Job has, but forbids harm to Job himself and later commands that Job's life be spared; Job acknowledges him as the one who gave and has taken away. He then answers Job out of the whirlwind, telling him to brace himself for questions. He presents himself as the one who laid the earth's foundations, shut the sea within doors and bounds, sends rain to empty wilderness, and provides prey for lions and ravens. He challenges Job to match his arm and thundering voice and points to behemoth, which he made. Job acknowledges that he can do all things and that none of his purposes is restrained. The LORD is angry with Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly of him as Job did, and commands a burnt offering. He accepts Job, restores his prosperity at twice the former amount, and blesses his latter end more than his beginning.

l: Satan, The Book of Job
s: Satan appears among God's sons presenting themselves before the LORD, reporting that he has been traveling back and forth on the earth. He accuses Job of fearing God only because of protection and blessings. Given power over Job's possessions but not Job himself, he brings about the loss of Job's goods and children. Appearing again, he argues Job would renounce God if his flesh were touched, and, given Job with his life spared, strikes him with painful sores.

l: sons (Job's sons), The Book of Job
s: Job's seven sons take turns feasting in their houses on birthdays, inviting their three sisters. Job sanctifies them and offers burnt offerings in case of sin. All die when a house collapses on them at their oldest brother's.

l: daughters (Job's daughters), The Book of Job
s: is_sibling_of Job's sons [three sisters] Job's three daughters are invited by their brothers to eat and drink at the birthday feasts. They are with their brothers in the oldest brother's house when it falls, and they die with them.

l: messengers (Job's four messengers), The Book of Job
s: Four messengers come to Job one after another, each speaking while the previous one is still talking. They report the Sabeans' raid on the oxen and donkeys, the fire of God burning the sheep and servants, the Chaldeans' seizure of the camels, and the death of Job's sons and daughters. Each says he alone has escaped to tell Job.

l: great wind (the wind that destroyed the house), The Book of Job
s: A great wind comes from the wilderness and strikes the four corners of the oldest brother's house. The house falls on the young men and they die, as the fourth messenger reports to Job.

l: wife (Job's wife), The Book of Job
s: Job's wife asks him whether he still maintains his integrity and tells him to renounce God and die. Job answers that she speaks like one of the foolish women.

l: Eliphaz the Temanite, The Book of Job
s: Eliphaz the Temanite is a friend of Job, one of three who come from Job's own place to sympathize and comfort him. He joins in weeping, tearing his robe, and sitting silently seven days and nights. He then speaks to Job in dialogue, first noting Job's past strengthening of others, arguing the innocent never perish while the wicked reap what they sow, and recounting a night vision in which a voice spoke of mortal injustice before God. Later he rebukes Job as a speaker of vain knowledge, appeals to the aged and tradition, and describes the wicked's ruin. In his last speech he accuses Job of great wickedness and urges return to the Almighty with promised restoration. Finally the LORD tells him his wrath is kindled against him and his two friends for not speaking rightly as Job did, and Eliphaz, with Bildad and Zophar, does as commanded.

l: Bildad the Shuhite, The Book of Job
s: Bildad the Shuhite is one of Job's three friends who come from his own place to comfort him, weeping, tearing his robe, and sitting silently seven days and nights. He then becomes a speaker in the dialogue, answering Job three times. He first rebukes Job's words and defends God's justice, claiming Job's children sinned and urging him to seek God and heed past generations. Later he protests being counted unclean and describes the wicked man's ruin. His last speech is short, stressing God's greatness and that man cannot be just before God. In the end the LORD's wrath falls on him, Eliphaz and Zophar for not speaking rightly, and Bildad does as the LORD commanded.

l: Zophar the Naamathite, The Book of Job
s: Zophar the Naamathite is one of Job's three friends who come from his own place to comfort him, weeping, tearing his robe and sitting silently seven days and nights. He then answers Job twice. First he rebukes Job's many words and mockery, doubts his claimed cleanness, calls God's mystery unfathomable, urges repentance and warns that the wicked have no escape. Then, stung by a reproof, he insists from ancient knowledge that the wicked man's triumph is brief and his ruin is his portion from God. At the end, the LORD's wrath falls on him with Eliphaz and Bildad for not speaking rightly, and he obeys the LORD's command.

l: three friends (Job's friends), The Book of Job
s: Job's three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite, come by appointment to comfort him; failing to recognize him, they weep, tear robes, scatter dust, and sit silently seven days, seeing his great grief.

l: Job's suffering, The Book of Job
s: Job's suffering is an evil that came upon him, marked by very great grief and bitterness, which he claims God caused without cause. It begins when Satan, with the LORD's permission but limited to sparing his life, strikes him with painful sores, worsened by his wife's urging to renounce God. Job then describes being broken by a storm, multiplied wounds, swiftly fleeing joyless days, and suffering that falls on blameless and wicked alike. It culminates in loss of glory and crown, uprooted hope, estrangement from family and friends, an emaciated body, and cries for justice unanswered.

l: God, The Book of Job
s: God, as portrayed across these records, is the Almighty and Holy One, Maker of man and ruler of the cosmos, discussed and addressed by Job, his friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar) and Elihu. What matters most is the dispute over his character: whether he is just and rewards each according to his ways, or, as Job claims, destroys blameless and wicked alike, hunts him, and writes bitter things against him. The records open with Eliphaz's vision: God distrusts even his servants and angels, and destroys those who sow trouble. He does countless unfathomable things, gives rain, exalts the lowly, frustrates the crafty and saves the needy. Job calls him the Almighty with arrows and terrors set against him, and a watcher of men who tests him constantly. Bildad insists God does not pervert justice, will not cast away the blameless or uphold evildoers. Job in turn describes God's power: removing mountains, shaking the earth, sealing the stars, stretching out the heavens, making the Bear, Orion and the Pleiades. Yet Job says God is not a man, has no umpire, fashioned and preserved him, knows he is not wicked, and still surrounds him with archers, a net and troops. Zophar says God exacts less than Job's iniquity deserves and that no one can oppose him. Job says wisdom, might, counsel and understanding are with him, and life and breath are in his hand. Later chapters stress that he dwells in the heights of heaven, judges the high, watches the mighty, has innumerable armies, hangs the earth on nothing, binds waters in clouds, strikes Rahab, and understands and established wisdom. Elihu presents him as Maker, greater than man, who speaks through dreams, finds a ransom, keeps souls from the pit, shows no partiality, sees all, hears the cry of the poor, and is unaffected by human sin or righteousness. He is mighty in understanding, an unmatched teacher, with unsearchable years, commanding rain, snow, ice, thunder and lightning, and does not regard the self-wise. Finally, he questions Job about the wild donkey and ostrich, and about Leviathan, whom none can stand before, declaring that everything under the heavens is his.

l: day of Job's birth, The Book of Job
s: is_cursed_to_be darkness [Job's wish] Job curses this day, asking that it perish and become darkness. He asks that God not seek it, that no light shine on it, and that a cloud, the shadow of death, and all that blackens the day terrify and claim it.

l: night of Job's conception, The Book of Job
s: The night Job was conceived, announced as a boy's conception, is cursed by Job in Chapter 3: he wishes it seized by darkness and barren, blaming it for not shutting his mother's womb or hiding trouble.

l: leviathan, The Book of Job
s: Leviathan is a fearsome creature described in Chapter 41 who cannot be caught, bound, tamed, traded, or made a servant, not even by Job. His sealed strong scales, stone-hard heart, strong neck, and terrifying teeth make him invulnerable, as swords, spears, arrows, and clubs count as nothing. He stirs the deep to boil, leaves trails like a threshing sledge, and is fearless and unequaled on earth, ending as king over all the sons of pride.

l: death, The Book of Job
s: Death, as spoken of by Job, is a place of quiet and rest that he longs for amid suffering. In Chapter 3 it is pictured as a leveling refuge: the wicked cease troubling, the weary rest, prisoners are at ease, servants are freed from masters, and kings, counselors, and infants who never saw light lie together. The miserable dig for it like hidden treasure. In Chapter 7 the emphasis shifts to finality: like a vanishing cloud, those going down to Sheol come up no more, never return home, and are no longer known, so Job would choose death over his suffering.

l: the miserable, The Book of Job
s: The miserable are those in bitter anguish; Job questions why they are given light and life. They long for death that does not come, seeking it above treasure, and rejoice finding the grave.

l: trouble, The Book of Job
s: Job says the night did not hide trouble from his eyes. He ends the chapter saying he has no ease, quiet, or rest, but trouble comes.

l: Job (the addressee of Eliphaz), The Book of Job
s: Job is a man addressed in successive speeches by Eliphaz, Zophar, and Elihu, with a final unit in which an unnamed listener is questioned about wild animals. Eliphaz first recalls that Job once instructed many and strengthened the weak, yet now faints under trouble, and he points to Job's piety and integrity as his confidence. Zophar quotes him as claiming pure doctrine and cleanness, calls him a boaster, says he deserves more punishment than God exacts, and urges him to set his heart right and put away iniquity, promising security and restoration. Eliphaz later charges him with vain words, hindering devotion, and speaking against God. Elihu says he is full of the judgment of the wicked, warns against wrath and bribes, says God would have drawn him out of distress, and tells him to magnify God's work. In the last unit, he is asked whether he understands or controls wild creatures. Over time, the address shifts from reminder to accusation to challenge.

l: spirit (seen by Eliphaz in a night vision), The Book of Job
s: has_appearance indiscernible form A spirit passed before Eliphaz's face, making the hair of his flesh stand up. It stood still with a form Eliphaz could not discern, and after silence a voice spoke.

l: those who plow iniquity and sow trouble, The Book of Job
